newsitem.title: CANADA: Exchanges crack down on small mining companies.
newsitem.headline: Exchanges crack down on small mining companies.

text.p: Officials at the Toronto, Vancouver and Alberta stock exchanges say Canada's sizzling start-up mining sector faces closer scrutiny after a series of wild stock market rides.

"There's no question there's increased surveillance," Neil Winchester, manager of surveillance for the Toronto Stock Exchange, said in a recent interview. "We're certainly watching them a lot more closely than we would have."
Canada's stock markets are among the world's top sources of financing for mining companies.
Regulators said they have been closely watching the small mining sector since last spring after two exploration companies flew out of control on the Alberta Stock Exchange.
Shares in Timbuktu Gold Corp. have been halted since April after the stock price soared to about C$30 ($22) from just pennies on preliminary drill results from Mali.
An investigation suggested that ore samples were probably tampered with and that the company's then president had past problems with regulators in the United States.
In May, Cartaway Resources Corp. plunged to C$2 ($1.46) from C$21 ($15.35) after disappointing drill results.
Although smaller mining stocks cooled off over the summer, they have heated up again this fall and exchange officials said they were taking extra precautions.

"Naturally, every exchange is afraid of what has happened in the past with Cartaway and Timbuktu," said Winchester. "That could very easily happen here. I'm not saying we're exempt from something like that."
The Toronto exchange, Canada's largest stock market, has been using geologists to double-check news releases.
Officials were also watching for exaggerated news that may come from companies trying to ride the coattails of big discoveries in Labrador, Indonesia and South America.
Recently the exchange halted the stocks of two smaller companies -- Atlanta Gold Corp. and Goldstake Explorations Inc. -- to take a closer look at results from Indonesia properties.
The Alberta exchange has introduced changes to restrict the involvement of brokerages in public offerings.
Vancouver officials are being more vigilant to ensure small mining companies do not overpromote their stocks, said Angela Huxham, in charge of surveillance at the exchange.
"We've got to be like that, because with junior companies there are problems in the market," she said. "We're very pro-active because we've got to be. It's a long haul."
But the problems of unscrupulous promoters are no worse than in the past, said Frank Giustra, president of Yorkton Securities.
"I think the problem is there have been so many great successes -- Bre-X, Diamond Fields, Arequipa," he said.
"When you have a market environment like that, any unscrupulous person who knows the business well enough can use it to their advantage by overly promoting."
